```rust
use knappnet::provenance::ENGINE_VERSION;

let run = compute_betweenness_approx(&g, &BetweennessApprox { samples: 5, seed: 3, ..Default::default() }, &Exec::default())?;
let p = &run.provenance;
let hex = |bytes: &[u8], k: usize| bytes.iter().take(k).map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect::<String>();
println!("measure {} revision {} engine {ENGINE_VERSION} seed {:?}", p.measure, p.revision, p.seed);
println!("parameter hash {}", hex(&p.params, 4));
println!("graph: {} nodes, {} ties, hash known before asking: {}", g.node_count(), g.edge_count(), p.graph.content().is_some());
let digest = hex(&g.content_hash(), 8);
println!("graph hash {digest}, known after asking: {}", p.graph.content().is_some());
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
measure betweenness_approx revision 1 engine 0.0.1 seed Some(3)
parameter hash 7bee3a7c
graph: 21 nodes, 190 ties, hash known before asking: false
graph hash ad4fe3bd37923e66, known after asking: true
```
:::

:::

Three things in the output.

**The graph hash is the same in two languages.** The engine's content hash covers the network as the engine holds it: whether ties have direction, whether they have weights, the number of nodes and of ties, then every tie's source and every tie's target in the order stored. The Python tab rebuilds that hash from the documented layout and gets the same 16 hexadecimal characters the Rust tab prints, so the hash is a checkable fact and not a private number. The layout carries a version tag ("knappnet graph content 1"), so treat a hash as comparable only between runs of the same tag. Notice what is in it: ties as positions. Change the order of the rows and the hash changes, which is why the previous section matters.

**The R graph hash is missing.** In the R tab the `graph hash` row is `NA`. I looked into why, and it is a gap in the engine's interface, not an error in your analysis. The engine computes a graph's content hash lazily, because hashing a very large graph costs more than computing a simple measure on it. A provenance record carries the hash only if something has already asked for it. The Rust tab shows exactly that: before `content_hash()` is called the record says it is unknown, and after the call the same record knows it. R's runtime path never makes that call (I also tried with the result cache switched off and after repeated runs: still missing), and the C interface that R goes through has no function to ask for the hash, so R cannot trigger it, and the field stays empty. Until that is fixed, do what the R tab does for the data: hash the file with `rlang::hash_file()`, and write the other fields in yourself. The other fields (measure, revision, parameter hash, seed, engine version) are filled in correctly in all languages, and the parameter hash printed by R and Rust is the same, so a result computed in R can be matched to the same call made from Rust.

**The engine does not know what you did around it.** It cannot record which file the ties came from, which rows you dropped, which package versions were loaded, or which random choices you made in your own code. The Python tab shows the minimum record for a library with no provenance of its own: the file's hash, the network's hash, the call with its seed, and the versions. Keep a record like it beside every table you hand to anybody, in a file, not in your head.

### Cache keys, and the size of the network

The engine uses the same ingredients for a different job. Its result cache is keyed on the graph, the measure, its revision, the parameter hash and the engine version, so a stored result is reused only if everything that could change it is the same. Anything you build to remember results (a notebook cache, a pipeline step) should key on the same list: the data hash, the code version, the parameters and the seed. If any of them changes, the stored answer is stale and must be computed again.

This is also what "reproducibility at scale" comes down to. A large network makes three things more expensive, and each has the same answer.

- **Hashing the data** costs a pass over every tie. Do it once, store it with the data, and compare it on load.
- **Sampled methods** (the sampled betweenness above, sampled paths, random walks) need their sample size and seed recorded, because they are the methods whose output moves most between runs.
- **Parallel runs**. The engine's documentation says its results do not depend on the number of threads, and it records the thread count in the provenance anyway. Where a tool does not make that promise, sums added in a different order differ in the last digits, as the betweenness comparison above showed. The next section is about what to do about that.

## Comparing outputs across tools {#sec-tolerance}

Suppose two tools disagree. The first question is not "which is right?" but "do they disagree by more than they should?" Floating-point numbers are not exact, and iterative methods stop before they have converged. A comparison needs a **tolerance**, a gap below which two numbers count as the same, chosen on purpose.

Three kinds of difference look alike and are not.

1. **Rounding.** Two correct programs add the same numbers in different orders and differ around $10^{-15}$ for values near 1. Use an absolute tolerance around $10^{-9}$ for scores that run from 0 to 1, and a relative one for scores that are large.
2. **Stopping rules.** An iterative method (eigenvector centrality, PageRank) stops when the change per round is small enough. A looser stopping rule leaves a larger error. NetworkX's PageRank stops at a tolerance of $10^{-6}$ by default, and the error against the exact answer can be larger than that number suggests.
3. **Scale and convention.** The same ranking scaled differently differs by a lot and agrees perfectly once rescaled. Eigenvector centrality is the classic: igraph scales so that the largest score is 1, NetworkX so that the scores have unit length.

The test below takes all three on Zachary's club. The **oracle** is an independent calculation that does not use either tool: for eigenvector centrality, the leading eigenvector of the adjacency matrix; for PageRank, the exact solution of the linear equations that define it, $(I - d P^{\top}) x = \frac{1 - d}{n}\mathbf{1}$, with $P$ the matrix of tie shares ($P_{ij} = A_{ij} / k_i$, where $k_i$ is $i$'s degree) and $d = 0.85$. Gaps smaller than $10^{-12}$ are shown as $10^{-12}$, since the digits below that are noise.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```r
# The oracle: the adjacency matrix, its leading eigenvector (unit length), and the exact PageRank solution.
A <- matrix(0, 34, 34)
A[cbind(karate_ties$source, karate_ties$target)] <- 1
A <- A + t(A)
top <- abs(eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE)$vectors[, 1])
oracle_eigen <- top / sqrt(sum(top^2))
oracle_rank <- solve(diag(34) - 0.85 * t(A / rowSums(A)), rep(0.15 / 34, 34))
gap <- \(a, b) max(abs(as.numeric(a) - as.numeric(b)))

tibble(
  check = c("eigenvector, igraph's scale", "eigenvector, unit length", "pagerank, tol 1e-6", "pagerank, tol 1e-12"),
  gap = c(gap(net_eigen(forward), oracle_eigen), gap(net_eigen(forward, convention = "networkx"), oracle_eigen),
          gap(net_pagerank(forward, tol = 1e-6), oracle_rank), gap(net_pagerank(forward, tol = 1e-12), oracle_rank))
) |>
  mutate(close_at_1e9 = gap < 1e-9, gap = signif(pmax(gap, 1e-12), 2))
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  check                           gap close_at_1e9
  <chr>                         <dbl> <lgl>       
1 eigenvector, igraph's scale 6.3e- 1 FALSE       
2 eigenvector, unit length    1  e-12 TRUE        
3 pagerank, tol 1e-6          2.5e- 7 FALSE       
4 pagerank, tol 1e-12         1  e-12 TRUE        
```
:::

## Python

```python
# The oracle: the adjacency matrix, its leading eigenvector (unit length), and the exact PageRank solution.
A = nx.to_numpy_array(forward, nodelist=members)
vectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)[1]
oracle_eigen = np.abs(vectors[:, -1]) / np.linalg.norm(vectors[:, -1])
oracle_rank = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(34) - 0.85 * (A / A.sum(axis=1)[:, None]).T, np.full(34, 0.15 / 34))
gap = lambda a, b: max(1e-12, float(np.abs(np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)).max()))

eig = nx.eigenvector_centrality_numpy(forward)
eig = np.array([eig[m] for m in members])  # NetworkX scales to unit length
rank = lambda tol: np.array([nx.pagerank(forward, tol=tol)[m] for m in members])
checks = [
    ("eigenvector, igraph's scale", eig, oracle_eigen / oracle_eigen.max()),  # compared without rescaling
    ("eigenvector, rescaled alike", eig / eig.max(), oracle_eigen / oracle_eigen.max()),
    ("pagerank, tol 1e-6 (default)", rank(1e-6), oracle_rank),
    ("pagerank, tol 1e-12", rank(1e-12), oracle_rank),
]
print(f"{'check':<31}{'gap':>9}  close at 1e-9")
for label, got, want in checks:
    print(f"{label:<31}{gap(got, want):>9.1e}  {np.allclose(got, want, rtol=0, atol=1e-9)}")
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
check                                gap  close at 1e-9
eigenvector, igraph's scale      6.3e-01  False
eigenvector, rescaled alike      1.0e-12  True
pagerank, tol 1e-6 (default)     4.5e-06  False
pagerank, tol 1e-12              1.0e-11  True
```
:::

## Rust

```rust
use knappnet::metrics::eigenvector::{compute_eigenvector_centrality, EigenScale, EigenvectorOptions};
use knappnet::metrics::spectral::{compute_pagerank, PagerankOptions};

// The oracle, written out: power iteration for the eigenvector (on A + I, which keeps it from
// oscillating) and PageRank iterated from its definition until nothing moves.
let mut degree = vec![0.0; 34];
for &(a, b) in &karate_ties { degree[a as usize] += 1.0; degree[b as usize] += 1.0; }
let mut oracle_eigen = vec![1.0; 34];
for _ in 0..2000 {
    let mut next = oracle_eigen.clone();
    for &(a, b) in &karate_ties { next[a as usize] += oracle_eigen[b as usize]; next[b as usize] += oracle_eigen[a as usize]; }
    let norm = next.iter().map(|v| v * v).sum::<f64>().sqrt();
    oracle_eigen = next.iter().map(|v| v / norm).collect();
}
let mut oracle_rank = vec![1.0 / 34.0; 34];
for _ in 0..2000 {
    let mut next = vec![0.15 / 34.0; 34];
    for &(a, b) in &karate_ties {
        next[b as usize] += 0.85 * oracle_rank[a as usize] / degree[a as usize];
        next[a as usize] += 0.85 * oracle_rank[b as usize] / degree[b as usize];
    }
    oracle_rank = next;
}
let gap = |a: &[f64], b: &[f64]| a.iter().zip(b).map(|(p, q)| (p - q).abs()).fold(0.0, f64::max).max(1e-12);
let eigen = |scale| compute_eigenvector_centrality(&forward, EigenvectorOptions { scale, ..Default::default() });
let rank = |tol: f64| compute_pagerank(&forward, &PagerankOptions { tol, ..Default::default() });

println!("{:<31}{:>9}  close at 1e-9", "check", "gap");
for (label, got, want) in [
    ("eigenvector, igraph's scale", eigen(EigenScale::Max)?.values, &oracle_eigen),
    ("eigenvector, unit length", eigen(EigenScale::Unit)?.values, &oracle_eigen),
    ("pagerank, tol 1e-6", rank(1e-6)?, &oracle_rank),
    ("pagerank, tol 1e-12", rank(1e-12)?, &oracle_rank),
] {
    let g = gap(&got, want);
    println!("{label:<31}{g:>9.1e}  {}", g < 1e-9);
}
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
check                                gap  close at 1e-9
eigenvector, igraph's scale       6.3e-1  false
eigenvector, unit length         1.0e-12  true
pagerank, tol 1e-6                2.5e-7  false
pagerank, tol 1e-12              1.0e-12  true
```
:::

:::

Read the table row by row. In R and Rust the first row compares the engine's default eigenvector scale (largest score 1) with an oracle of unit length, so the gap is large and the check fails: the numbers are not wrong, they are in different units. The second row asks for the other scale and the gap is at the rounding floor. In the Python tab the same lesson runs the other way: NetworkX's unit-length answer fails against an oracle scaled to a maximum of 1, and passes once both sides are rescaled alike.

The PageRank rows show the stopping rule. With a loose tolerance (NetworkX's default of $10^{-6}$ in Python, the same value in the engine) the answer is good to about six or seven digits, not nine, and a test with tolerance $10^{-9}$ fails. With a tight tolerance it passes. Neither tool has a bug. They stop at different places, so a comparison tolerance has to be looser than the loosest stopping rule in play, or you have to tighten the stopping rule first.

How to choose, in practice:

- Pick the tolerance *before* looking at the gap, and say what it was. A tolerance chosen after the fact only ever says that the numbers you have are close to the numbers you have.
- Use an absolute tolerance for scores bounded by 1, a relative tolerance for scores that can be large, and both together (`rtol` and `atol`) when a score can be zero.
- Compare after putting the two results on the same scale, same direction, same node order and same convention. Most "failures" are one of these.
- Compare rankings separately from values. Two tools can agree on every rank and differ in the fourth decimal, which is usually fine, or agree to ten decimals and differ on a tie.

### Testing against oracles

A test is a comparison you can rerun. Three kinds of oracle earn their keep, in the order of how much I trust them.

1. **A hand calculation on a tiny network.** Five people in a line, numbered 1 to 5, have betweenness $0, 3, 4, 3, 0$: person 3 is the only route for four pairs of others (1 and 4, 1 and 5, 2 and 4, 2 and 5), and person 2 is the only route for three pairs (1 with 3, 4 and 5). If a tool cannot reproduce numbers you can verify on paper, no amount of agreement with other tools should reassure you. @sec-getting-started starts with this habit, and it is the chapter's central one.
2. **An independent calculation.** The linear-algebra checks above. They share no code with the tool under test, so a shared bug is unlikely.
3. **Another tool, with the convention matched.** Useful, but two tools can share a convention and a bug, and the match is only as good as your care in matching.

Put these in a test file, run it when you upgrade a package, and keep it in the project (see below). In R, `testthat::expect_equal(x, y, tolerance = 1e-9)` does the comparison; in Python, `numpy.testing.assert_allclose(x, y, rtol=0, atol=1e-9)` or `pytest.approx`; in Rust, an `assert!((a - b).abs() < 1e-9)` inside a `#[test]` function. The knappnet repository tests its measures against NetworkX, igraph, sna and hand-worked values in this way, which is why its documentation can say which convention each tool uses.

## A project you can rerun

Everything above is about what to record. This section is about where to put it, so that a rerun is a command and not an excavation. None of it is exotic. The advice is the same set of habits that the literature on reproducible computing keeps converging on [@peng2011reproducible; @sandve2013ten; @wilson2017good], applied to network data.

### Layout

One folder per analysis, with the same few places in the same order every time.

```text
karate-study/
  README.md          what this is, how to rerun it, who to ask
  data/
    raw/             files exactly as received; never edited
    clean/           files made by code from raw/, and the code that made them
  code/
    01-build-network.R
    02-measures.R
    03-report.qmd
  tests/             hand-worked and oracle checks (see above)
  results/           tables and figures made by the code; safe to delete and regenerate
  renv.lock          the R packages and versions (or requirements.lock, Cargo.lock)
  provenance.json    data hashes, seeds, conventions, versions, one record per run
```

Three rules do most of the work. **Raw data are read-only**: if you have to fix a typo, fix it in code that reads `raw/` and writes `clean/`, so the fix is visible and repeatable. **Everything in `results/` can be deleted and rebuilt** from `code/` and `data/`; if it cannot, something is missing from the record. **Numbered scripts** run in order from a clean session, so "run all" is the whole analysis and no step depends on something you did by hand.

### Notebooks and Quarto

A notebook mixes code, results and prose in one file, which is good for explaining and bad for reproducing, because the order you ran the cells in is not saved. Quarto (the tool this book is made with) has two settings that help. First, it runs the document from top to bottom in a fresh session, which catches hidden state. Second, it can store the results of expensive code and rerun only what changed. In the project file that is a line like `execute: freeze: auto`. Check Quarto's current documentation for the exact spelling, since options change.

A short header for any analysis notebook, in any language:

1. Set the seed **once, at the top**, in a cell you do not reorder, and also pass it explicitly to any call that takes one.
2. Print the versions you rely on, in the notebook itself (`sessionInfo()` in R, the package versions in Python, the engine version in Rust), so they are in the output people read.
3. Print the hash of every input file next to its name.
4. Read the data from a path relative to the project folder, never from `C:\Users\you\Downloads`.

### Lockfiles and containers

A **lockfile** lists the exact versions of every package your analysis used. `renv.lock` does it for R (`renv::snapshot()` writes it, `renv::restore()` reads it), `uv lock` or a pinned `requirements.txt` for Python, and `Cargo.lock` for Rust (commit it, and build with `--locked` so a changed lockfile is an error). A lockfile fixes the packages. It does not fix R, Python or the operating system.

A **container** goes one step further: it packages the operating system, the language and the packages as one image that runs the same on any machine with a container runtime. A minimal recipe looks like this. It is a pattern, not something this book builds, so check the base image tag against what is current.

```dockerfile
# Pin the image by version, not "latest": "latest" is a moving target.
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.1
WORKDIR /project
COPY renv.lock renv.lock
RUN R -e "install.packages('renv'); renv::restore()"
COPY . .
CMD ["Rscript", "code/02-measures.R"]
```

Containers and lockfiles solve *the same* problem from two sides, and neither solves the problems of the earlier sections. A container will happily run a script that reads sorted-by-accident data, draws from the wrong seed, or uses another tool's convention. They keep the environment still while the analysis does its work; the work still has to be reproducible.

When a pinned environment is too much, the lighter habit is enough for most projects: a lockfile, the version numbers in the output, and a test file that fails loudly when an upgrade changes a number.

## Sharing data without sharing people {#sec-sharing}

To reproduce your result someone needs your network. That network has people in it. A **node-and-tie file with names removed** feels anonymous and usually is not, because a network identifies people by their position in it, and positions are a much richer fingerprint than most people expect. Two studies made the point sharply: attackers who could plant or already knew a small part of a network could find specific people in an "anonymized" one [@backstrom2007wherefore], and a second network with overlapping members could be used to re-identify people in the first [@narayanan2009deanonymizing].

You can measure the risk on your own data before you share it. Suppose an outsider knows a member's degree, and perhaps the degrees of that member's friends. How many members are the *only* one that fits? The idea is **k-anonymity** [@sweeney2002kanonymity]: a published record is k-anonymous when at least k people share its description, so a description that fits exactly one person has $k = 1$ and identifies them. Count it for the karate club.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```r
# What could an outsider look for? Count how many members share each description.
degree <- rowSums(A)
describe <- list(
  `degree` = as.character(degree),
  `degree and friends' degrees` = map_chr(1:34, \(m) paste(degree[m], paste(sort(degree[A[m, ] > 0]), collapse = ","), sep = "|")),
  `degree in bands of five` = as.character(degree %/% 5)
)
tibble(
  what_an_outsider_knows = names(describe),
  unique_members = map_int(describe, \(s) sum(table(s)[s] == 1)),
  smallest_group = map_int(describe, \(s) min(table(s)))
)
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  what_an_outsider_knows      unique_members smallest_group
  <chr>                                <int>          <int>
1 degree                                   6              1
2 degree and friends' degrees             23              1
3 degree in bands of five                  0              2
```
:::

## Python

```python
# What could an outsider look for? Count how many members share each description.
degree_of = dict(forward.degree())
descriptions = {
    "degree": lambda m: (degree_of[m],),
    "degree and friends' degrees": lambda m: (degree_of[m], tuple(sorted(degree_of[u] for u in forward[m]))),
    "degree in bands of five": lambda m: (degree_of[m] // 5,),
}
print(f"{'what an outsider knows':<30}{'unique members':>15}{'smallest group':>16}")
for label, describe in descriptions.items():
    groups = Counter(describe(m) for m in members)
    print(f"{label:<30}{sum(groups[describe(m)] == 1 for m in members):>15}{min(groups.values()):>16}")
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
what an outsider knows         unique members  smallest group
degree                                      6               1
degree and friends' degrees                23               1
degree in bands of five                     0               2
```
:::

## Rust

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

// What could an outsider look for? Count how many members share each description.
let mut neighbors: Vec<Vec<usize>> = vec![Vec::new(); 34];
for &(a, b) in &karate_ties { neighbors[a as usize].push(b as usize); neighbors[b as usize].push(a as usize); }
let own: Vec<usize> = neighbors.iter().map(|n| n.len()).collect();
let descriptions: Vec<(&str, Vec<Vec<usize>>)> = vec![
    ("degree", (0..34).map(|m| vec![own[m]]).collect()),
    ("degree and friends' degrees", (0..34).map(|m| {
        let mut d = vec![own[m]];
        let mut friends: Vec<usize> = neighbors[m].iter().map(|&u| own[u]).collect();
        friends.sort();
        d.extend(friends);
        d
    }).collect()),
    ("degree in bands of five", (0..34).map(|m| vec![own[m] / 5]).collect()),
];
println!("{:<30}{:>15}{:>16}", "what an outsider knows", "unique members", "smallest group");
for (label, d) in &descriptions {
    let mut groups: HashMap<&Vec<usize>, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for key in d { *groups.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1; }
    let unique = d.iter().filter(|key| groups[key] == 1).count();
    println!("{label:<30}{unique:>15}{:>16}", groups.values().min().unwrap());
}
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
what an outsider knows         unique members  smallest group
degree                                      6               1
degree and friends' degrees                23               1
degree in bands of five                     0               2
```
:::

:::

Reading the table: a few members are the only ones with their degree, and with the degrees of their friends added, most members are unique. An outsider who knew only that someone has a handful of friends with particular numbers of friends could pick that person out. Coarsening the description (here, degree in bands of five) leaves no one unique and no group smaller than two, but it also throws away detail, and bands are a rough remedy, not a guarantee. A guarantee is a harder problem than counting, and nobody should call a network anonymous because the names were dropped.

Practical rules, from the least to the most protective:

- **Ask whether you need to share the network at all.** Often the measures and a hash of the data are enough, and the data stay with their owner. A hash proves you ran the same data without showing it.
- **Share a replacement network when you can**: a model fitted to the data, or a simulation with the same size, density and degrees, kept clearly separate from the real thing.
- **Replace names by random ids**, drawn once and kept private. Do not make an id from the name with a plain hash: for a short list of known names, anyone can hash every candidate name and look for a match. A secret random id has no such shortcut.
- **Remove or coarsen attributes** that make a person stand out (rare job titles, exact ages, small places), and test with the counting above.
- **Check consent and ethics first**, and follow the rules of whoever collected the data. @sec-collecting-data covers what the people in the network were told.

None of this guarantees privacy, and I have no number that says how much is enough. What it gives you is a habit: before sharing, ask how someone who knows a little could find someone in the file.

## A checklist you can paste into a project

Everything in this chapter fits on a page. Copy this into your `README.md`.

1. **Data.** Raw file kept read-only; its hash recorded; the rule for turning it into a network written in code.
2. **Network.** Directed or not; what happens to repeated ties, loops and ties both ways; ids that belong to people, starting at 0 or at 1 (say which).
3. **Order.** Nodes sorted by id before anything that uses position; ranked lists cut with the tie in view.
4. **Randomness.** Seed set once and passed explicitly; number of draws; the tool that drew them; results repeated with at least two other seeds.
5. **Conventions.** One line per measure naming the convention (and every non-default parameter); never compare tools before matching them.
6. **Tolerance.** The tolerance used to compare outputs, and what it was compared against (hand calculation, independent calculation or another tool).
7. **Provenance.** Measure and revision, parameter hash, engine or library version, graph hash and file hash, saved next to the result.
8. **Environment.** Lockfile committed; versions printed in the notebook; a container if others will rerun it.
9. **Tests.** A file that checks at least one hand-worked answer and fails loudly after an upgrade.
10. **Sharing.** Who can see the network, what an outsider who knew a little could learn, and what you removed.

## Cards for programs {#sec-repro-cards}

The cards that ship with this book (@sec-reporting explains them) now include three for this chapter. `reproducible-run` is the checklist above, in the form a program can check before it reports a result. `cross-tool-comparison` says how to compare two tools' numbers: match the convention, rescale, pick the tolerance first, and test the ranking separately. `sharing-network-data` says what to count and what to remove before a file leaves your hands. A program that runs knappnet should read them before it writes a sentence about a result, and should refuse to say that a result "reproduces" without the items they list.

## Where tools disagree, and what we did about it

A summary of what this chapter found, for the "where tools disagree" habit from the earlier chapters.

- **Repeated ties and loops.** One tie list gave densities of 0.50, 0.40 and 0.30 depending on whether repeats and loops are kept. The engine reads the list as recorded, like igraph; NetworkX's `Graph` merges and keeps loops; sna and UCINET read a matrix.
- **Random draws.** The same seed starts different streams in R, Python (`random`), NumPy and the engine. R and Rust agree because they call the same engine. NetworkX's `gnm_random_graph` and sampled betweenness (`k=`) make different draws than the engine for the same seed.
- **Closeness on a network with pieces.** Four conventions, three different leaders (igraph F and G, NetworkX and UCINET C, sna nobody).
- **Eigenvector scale.** igraph's largest score is 1; NetworkX's, sna's and UCINET's vector has unit length.
- **PageRank stopping.** NetworkX's default tolerance stops with an error near $10^{-6}$ against the exact answer; the engine's default tolerance is tighter, and its tolerance can be loosened to match.
- **Graph hash in R.** Missing from the provenance record (see above); present in Rust and reproducible in Python by hand.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Setting the seed makes it reproducible."** Only for the same code, the same tool and the same order of draws. It does nothing about a changed file, a reordered table or another package's recipe.
- **"If two tools differ, one has a bug."** More often they use different conventions or stop at different tolerances. Check the convention first.
- **"A container makes it reproducible."** It makes the environment reproducible. The analysis can still depend on row order, an unrecorded seed or a file that changed.
- **"A hash proves the result is right."** It proves the input is the same. A wrong analysis on the right data has a perfectly good hash.
- **"Removing the names anonymizes the network."** Positions identify people. Count the unique descriptions before you believe it.
- **"I'll write it down later."** The seed, the data version and the convention are the three things nobody can reconstruct afterwards.

## Exercises

1. **By hand.** Five people: Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev, Eli. The recorded ties are Ana-Ben, Ben-Chloe, Chloe-Ana, Ben-Chloe (again) and Dev-Dev. Find every person's degree and the density, as recorded and as a simple graph that keeps the loop. Check that the degrees add up to twice the number of ties.
2. **By hand.** Three people, A, B, C, with ties A to B and B to C, read as arrows. How many ties does each person have if you read the same list as undirected pairs? Now add the arrow B to A. What changes for the arrow reading and for the pair reading?
3. **By hand.** The Park-Miller generator starts from seed 1 and applies $s \leftarrow 16807 \, s \bmod 2147483647$. Find the first two numbers in the stream (before dividing by 2147483647), and the number after dividing, to four decimal places for the second.
4. **Coding.** Rerun the order check on the karate club with a third listing: members sorted by name in reverse alphabetical order of the string ("9" after "34"). Does the top six by degree change again? Does Louvain with seed 1?
5. **Coding.** In the closeness table, add a fifth reading, harmonic centrality (@sec-centrality). Is its leader one of the four from the table, and why does it avoid the problem?
6. **Coding.** Write the hand-worked betweenness test for five people in a line, $0, 3, 4, 3, 0$, in your language of choice with a tolerance of $10^{-9}$, and run it against the engine or NetworkX.
7. **Interpretation.** A colleague reruns your community analysis and gets four groups where you reported four, but a different member of the club is in a different group. Which questions do you ask, in order, before deciding who is right?
8. **Interpretation.** A report says "closeness was computed in R, so the numbers match the book." Name two things that could still differ.
9. **Interpretation.** You are asked to publish the friendship network of a 40-person department with names replaced by ids. List three checks you would run, one question you would ask the people in the network, and one thing you would offer to share instead.
10. **Design.** Write a provenance record for your own last analysis. Which fields could you fill from the output alone, and which had to come from you?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers

1. As recorded: Ana 2, Ben 3, Chloe 3, Dev 2 (a loop adds 2), Eli 0; the sum is 10, twice the 5 ties; density is $5/10 = 0.50$. As a simple graph that keeps the loop: the repeated Ben-Chloe is merged, so Ana 2, Ben 2, Chloe 2, Dev 2, Eli 0, sum 8, twice the 4 ties; density $4/10 = 0.40$.
2. Read as undirected pairs, A has 1 tie, B has 2 and C has 1. With the extra arrow B to A, the arrow reading has 3 ties (A to B, B to C, B to A) and a mutual pair, while the pair reading still has 2 ties, because A-B was already there. The arrow reading changes; the pair reading does not. That is why "how many ties" needs the reading stated.
3. The first number is $16807 \times 1 \bmod 2147483647 = 16807$. The second is $16807^2 = 282475249$, which is below 2147483647, so it stays 282475249; divided by 2147483647 it is 0.1315 (0.13153778 before rounding). (You can check against the tabs: the first three numbers they print are 0.000, 0.132 and 0.756.)
4. The degrees do not change, so members 4 and 32 are still tied for sixth place. In this listing member 4 comes before member 32 (as strings, "4" sorts after "32", so in reverse order it is listed first), so the top six is the same as in the forward listing: 34, 1, 33, 3, 2 and 4. The tie was settled by where each member happened to be listed, not by anything about the members. For Louvain, run it with seed 1 and compare the groups with the forward run by adjusted Rand; whatever you get is one more draw from the near-equal partitions.
5. Harmonic centrality adds $1/d$ over everyone and treats an unreachable person as $1/\infty = 0$, so a person on a tiny island scores low without any special rule. In the split network its leader is C, the same as NetworkX's and UCINET's. It avoids the problem because it never divides by the number of people reached.
6. In Python: build `nx.path_graph(5)` and `np.testing.assert_allclose(list(nx.betweenness_centrality(g, normalized=False).values()), [0, 3, 4, 3, 0], atol=1e-9)`. Check the numbers by hand first: the pairs of other people whose only route passes through person 3 are (1,4), (1,5), (2,4) and (2,5), giving 4; person 2 is on the routes of (1,3), (1,4) and (1,5), giving 3.
7. First, were both runs on the same file (compare hashes) and the same order of nodes? Second, the same seed, the same tool and the same version? Third, the same resolution and weights? If all three match, the groupings are two valid draws, and you compare them with adjusted Rand and report what is stable. Only if the inputs are identical and the outputs still differ do you suspect a bug.
8. The convention (closeness has four), the handling of repeated ties and loops, the direction, the version of the package, and the tolerance of any iterative method.
9. Checks: how many members are unique by degree, and by degree plus friends' degrees; whether rare attributes (a unique job title) are present; whether anyone outside the department could match the network against another data set. Question to the people: whether they agreed to this use, and what they were told. Offer instead: the measures and a hash of the data, or a simulated network with the same size and degrees.
10. Fields that come from the output: the measure, its revision, the parameter hash, the engine or library version, the seed if you passed one, and the graph hash where the tool provides it. Fields that come from you: the data file and its hash, the rule for building the network, the convention you chose, the random choices in your own code, and the checks you ran.
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Network results fail to reproduce for eight usual reasons: how repeated ties, loops and direction are read; random draws; seeds that mean different things in different tools; the order of nodes and ties; conventions; stopping rules and rounding; software versions; and changed data. A seed makes a run repeatable in one tool, not portable across tools, and the answer should not depend on the draw. Give every node an id that belongs to the person, sort by it, and cut ranked lists with the ties in view. Compare tools with a tolerance chosen before you look, on the same scale and convention, and test against a hand-worked answer. Record the data hash, the graph hash, the parameters, the seed and the versions next to every result, and keep a lockfile, a test and, when others will rerun it, a container. Before sharing a network, count how many people an outsider could single out. The one-line takeaway: write down the seed, the convention and the data version, because nobody can reconstruct them later.
:::

## Further reading

For why computational results should come with their code and data, and how, @peng2011reproducible, @sandve2013ten and @wilson2017good. For the random-number generators in this chapter, @parkmiller1988random and @salmon2011parallel, and for the hash function behind the engine's graph hash, @aumasson2013blake2. For colour refinement and the structure hash, @shervashidze2011weisfeiler. For the conventions of the tools compared here, @csardi2006igraph, @hagberg2008exploring, @butts2008sna and @borgatti2002ucinet. For how identities leak from "anonymous" networks, @backstrom2007wherefore and @narayanan2009deanonymizing, and for k-anonymity, @sweeney2002kanonymity. For what to write once the result is reproducible, @sec-reporting, and for where the data came from, @sec-collecting-data.
